title: Variability is induced by changed conditions acting on the reproductive system

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Variability is induced by changed conditions acting on the reproductive system

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Deviations of structure arise in some way from the conditions of life to which parents and their ancestors have been exposed over several generations, acting chiefly by disturbing the reproductive system; hence variability is greater under domestication or cultivation than in nature.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But the much greater variability, as well as the greater frequency of monstrosities, under domestication or cultivation, than under nature, leads me to believe that deviations of structure are in some way due to the nature of the conditions of life, to which the parents and their more remote ancestors have been exposed during several generations.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter V, “Laws of Variation”; section “Effects of external conditions.”. Scope: plants and animals, domesticated and wild

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch05-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.58

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern genomics can compare variability and test environmental effects in particular systems. Existing observational data poorly isolate changed conditions acting through the reproductive system from demographic and selective causes.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare mutation, recombination, developmental anomaly and phenotypic-variance rates in matched wild and domesticated populations across multigenerational environmental histories. Higher heritable novelty after altered conditions, mediated by germline changes, supports the mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Historical ancestral environments and germline disturbance are rarely measured directly.

Domestication includes bottlenecks, admixture and deliberate selection.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A domestic-versus-wild variance contrast is measurable, but the proposed cause, disturbance of the reproductive system by changed conditions, needs a mutation-rate design that existing trait databases do not contain. Public sequences and trait compilations cover some crops and livestock and leave the mechanism entangled with relaxed selection and sampling. The feasible study is a partial proxy, not a direct test of induced germline disturbance.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare within-population phenotypic variance and germline mutation rate between domesticated populations and wild relatives, and test whether novel conditions raise mutation specifically in the reproductive lineage. Greater domestic variance and a condition-dependent germline mutation increase would support the claim; equal variances after observation effort and population size are controlled, or mutation rates unaffected by conditions, would refute the corresponding clause.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Domesticates are observed more carefully and kept in larger or more subdivided populations, which inflates apparent variability.

Relaxed selection and new mutations are different causes of the same extra variance.

Paired within-population variances and condition-dependent mutation rates are scattered.
